questions.q: Côte d'Or growers plant around ten thousand vines to the hectare. What follows for the crop each vine carries?
questions.exp: Close planting makes each vine compete with its neighbours for water and nutrients, so it grows less vigorously, roots deeper and carries a small crop of more concentrated fruit; the permitted yield then falls as the tier rises. The consequence is cost: rows a metre apart need straddle tractors and a great deal of handwork, which the Court asks a Certified candidate to weigh.

questions.q: Red Burgundy is traditionally raised in the pièce. How many litres does that barrel hold?
questions.exp: The Burgundian pièce holds 228 litres, a little more than the 225 litre Bordeaux barrique; Chablis keeps a half-size cask of its own, the feuillette. Red Burgundy spends twelve to eighteen months in the pièce after a cold soak and fermentation in open vats, with the share of new oak rising from village to grand cru.

questions.q: Oak in Chablis rises with rank. At which level is a grower most likely to ferment or age part of the wine in barrel?
questions.exp: Petit Chablis and village Chablis are raised almost entirely in steel to keep their green apple and saline edge, while many premier and grand cru wines spend part of their time in barrel, usually old wood that adds texture rather than toast. The Court asks this gradient alongside the Mâconnais one (Mâcon-Villages in steel, Pouilly-Fuissé often in barrel) and the Beaujolais one.

questions.q: A guest wants a Burgundian dish for a village Pommard. Which classic, braised in red wine with lardons, mushrooms and small onions, is the regional match?
questions.exp: Coq au vin, like boeuf bourguignon, is braised in red Burgundy, and the Pinot Noir's bright acidity and moderate tannin meet the sauce without overwhelming the meat. Bouillabaisse belongs to Provence and its rosé, and choucroute and tarte flambée to Alsace; Chablis or Aligoté goes with the Burgundian snails and gougères.

questions.q: Which of these climats is one of the seven Chablis Grands Crus?
questions.exp: The seven Chablis Grands Crus, all on one slope on the right bank of the Serein facing southwest, are Blanchot, Bougros, Les Clos, Grenouilles, Preuses, Valmur and Vaudésir. Montée de Tonnerre, Fourchaume and Vaillons are among the important Premiers Crus the Court also asks a Certified candidate to recognise.

questions.q: Richebourg and Romanée-Saint-Vivant are Grands Crus within which Côte de Nuits village?
questions.exp: Vosne-Romanée holds the densest cluster of great red sites in Burgundy: Romanée-Conti, La Romanée, La Tâche, Richebourg, Romanée-Saint-Vivant and La Grande Rue, with Échezeaux and Grands-Échezeaux in neighbouring Flagey. The Court's Certified cell asks every Côte de Nuits village with the Grands Crus it holds.

questions.q: The Court names Raveneau and Dauvissat among the Burgundy domaines to know. Where do they make their wine?
questions.exp: Raveneau and Dauvissat are Chablis domaines, famed for premier and grand cru wines raised in old barrels, and the Court sets them beside the Côte d'Or's great domaines and the large négociants such as Louis Jadot, Louis Latour and Joseph Drouhin. A domaine grows its own grapes; a négociant buys grapes or wine and bottles them under its own name.

questions.q: Marc de Bourgogne, the region's own brandy, is distilled from what?
questions.exp: Marc is distilled from the pomace, the skins, pips and stems left after pressing, and Marc de Bourgogne is usually aged in oak before release; Italy's equivalent is grappa. It is the spirit that washes the rind of Époisses, and the Court names it in its Non-Wine Production row for Burgundy.
